question.text: A 36-year-old man presents to a physician after having a transient loss of consciousness while resting after dinner the previous night. His symptoms only lasted for a few seconds and resolved spontaneously. This is the third time he experienced such an episode. He says that he recently started having nightmares. His father died of sudden cardiac death at the age of 45 years without a history of hypertension or any chronic cardiac disorder. A complete physical examination was normal. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevations in V1, V2, and V3, and the presence of incomplete right bundle branch block (RBBB). After a complete diagnostic evaluation, Brugada syndrome was diagnosed. He has prescribed a class I anti-arrhythmic drug, which is a sodium channel blocker that slows phase 0 depolarization in ventricular muscle fibers. The drug also blocks potassium channels and prolongs action potential duration, but it does not shorten phase 3 repolarization. The drug also has mild anticholinergic and alpha-blocking activity. If taken in high doses, which of the following are the most likely side effects of the drug?

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is prescribed a class I anti-arrhythmic drug, which is a sodium channel blocker. Common side effects of these drugs, especially at higher doses, include headache and tinnitus due to the drug's anticholinergic effects. While other side effects are possible, headache and tinnitus are the most likely and commonly reported.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The drug is a class I anti-arrhythmic, which are known to cause headache and tinnitus.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Pulmonary fibrosis and corneal deposits are more associated with certain other anti-arrhythmic drugs (e.g., amiodarone). Pedal edema and flushing are more typical of beta-blockers. Hypothyroidism and phototoxicity are not commonly associated with class I anti-arrhythmics.

rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered other anti-arrhythmic classes (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers) which have different side effect profiles, but the prescribed drug's specific mechanism points to headache and tinnitus as the most likely side effects.

The other options describe side effects of drugs not relevant to this case (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis from amiodarone, hypothyroidism from propylthiouracil, or phototoxicity from certain antibiotics).

qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other antiarrhythmics like amiodarone (pulmonary fibrosis), beta-blockers (bradycardia), or calcium channel blockers (hypotension) were considered but ruled out based on the drug’s described pharmacology and the clinical context of Brugada syndrome.
